title: Famous Hangover Cures: Anthony Bourdain's and Others, Checked
excerpt: Anthony Bourdain's hangover cure, the prairie oyster, Kingsley Amis's advice, the Corpse Reviver and the world's hangover soups, checked one by one: what helps, what backfires, and what actually works.
metaDescription: Anthony Bourdain's hangover cure, the prairie oyster, the Bloody Mary and hangover soups checked: what each famous remedy gets right and wrong.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Anthony Bourdain's famous hangover cure (usually quoted as Advil, a large cold Coca-Cola, a joint, and a big bowl of spicy Sichuan food) is partly sensible and partly just a good line. The ibuprofen and the Coke can genuinely take the edge off a headache and an empty tank. The spicy food and the joint are personal taste, and for a queasy stomach they can backfire. The same pattern runs through almost every famous hangover cure, from Jeeves's prairie oyster to the Corpse Reviver: each one contains one or two things that help a little (fluid, salt, sugar, caffeine, a painkiller, food) wrapped in a lot of ritual. None of them cures a hangover, because nothing does. There is no good evidence that any single food, drink, or remedy reverses one. What helps is time, sleep, fluids, food, and drinking less next time.

This guide goes through the best-known celebrity, literary, and cultural hangover cures one by one, explains what's in each that might actually work, and flags the parts that could make you feel worse.

**The quick scorecard:** Bourdain's cure gets a pass on the Advil and Coke, a "your call" on the Sichuan food, and a no on the joint for most people. The prairie oyster is mostly a dare. Every "hair of the dog" cocktail (the Bloody Mary or the Corpse Reviver) only delays the hangover. The traditional hangover soups from around the world, such as menudo, haejangguk, and pho, are the best of the lot, because they deliver fluid, salt, and easy food at once.

> **When a hangover is something more.** A normal hangover fades over the course of the day. **Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US) if** someone can't keep any fluids down for many hours, is vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, is confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake, has a seizure, has slow or irregular breathing, or has chest pain or a racing heart that won't settle. Those can be signs of alcohol poisoning, severe dehydration, or another emergency, not a hangover. And if you get shaky, sweaty, and anxious on mornings after drinking and a drink is the only thing that settles it, that's worth an honest conversation with a doctor. It can be an early sign of alcohol withdrawal rather than an ordinary hangover.

## Why Famous Hangover Cures Never Quite Work

Before checking individual cures, it helps to know what a hangover actually is, because that explains why every famous remedy falls short.

A hangover isn't one problem. It's several at once:

- **Fluid and salt loss.** Alcohol blocks a hormone (vasopressin) that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate more. You can wake up thirsty and light-headed.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up sleep in the second half of the night, especially the dreaming stage. You wake up tired no matter how many hours you were in bed.
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response that has been linked to the aches, low mood, and "flu-like" feeling of a hangover.
- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before breaking it down further. It's thought to contribute to nausea and the general poisoned feeling, although researchers still debate how big its role is in a typical hangover.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol inflames the stomach lining and increases acid, which is where the nausea and heartburn come from.
- **Low blood sugar.** Drinking can lower blood sugar, which adds to shakiness, weakness, and fatigue.
- **Congeners.** Dark drinks like whiskey, red wine, and brandy carry more of these by-products of fermentation and aging, which may make hangovers worse.

Every famous cure tends to target one or two of these, rarely all of them, and none speeds up the core recovery process. That's why a careful 2005 systematic review in the *BMJ* (Pittler and colleagues) looked at the controlled trials of hangover remedies available at the time and concluded there was no compelling evidence that any of them prevented or treated hangovers. Later research has turned up a few promising leads, but the overall picture hasn't changed much: you can ease symptoms, but you can't skip the recovery.

With that in mind, here's how the famous cures stack up.

## Anthony Bourdain's Hangover Cure

The late chef, writer, and TV host Anthony Bourdain gave the most-quoted hangover formula of modern times. It's usually repeated as: **Advil, a large cold Coca-Cola, a joint, and a big bowl of spicy Sichuan food.** The exact wording varies a little depending on where you read it, but those four parts are always there. It's popular because it sounds like him: practical, a bit outlaw, and built around great food.

Here's each part, checked.

### Advil (ibuprofen): the most useful part

Ibuprofen is a real, effective pain reliever, and a hangover headache is real pain. It also works against inflammation, which is one of the drivers of hangover misery. If you're going to take one thing from the Bourdain cure, this is it.

The caveats matter, though. Alcohol already irritates your stomach, and ibuprofen can too. The label warns about stomach bleeding for people who have three or more drinks a day. After a big night you're also likely to be a bit dehydrated, which is when ibuprofen is harder on the kidneys. So take a single label dose, with food and a full glass of water, and skip it if you have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or take blood thinners. Don't take it before bed "to get ahead of" the headache, while alcohol is still in your stomach. For a full side-by-side, see our guide to [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover).

### A large cold Coca-Cola: better than it sounds

A cold Coke delivers three useful things at once: fluid, quick sugar, and a modest amount of caffeine. The fluid helps with dehydration. The sugar helps if your blood sugar is low. The caffeine can ease the drowsy, foggy feeling, and for regular coffee drinkers, it heads off a caffeine-withdrawal headache stacking on top of the hangover headache.

Some people also find that small sips of a cold, fizzy, sweet drink settle mild nausea. That's a common folk observation rather than a proven treatment, but it's harmless for most people.

The limits: a regular Coke has no meaningful salt or potassium, so it doesn't replace what you lost the way an oral rehydration drink does, and the acidity can bother a sore stomach. Pair it with water. And don't count on caffeine to "fix" you. It masks tiredness; it doesn't undo poor sleep.

### A joint: the part to skip

This is the part that gets quoted most and holds up worst. Some people say cannabis eases their nausea and helps them rest. But there's no good evidence that it treats a hangover, and there are good reasons to be cautious:

- It's illegal in many places, and even where it's legal, it can impair you for driving and work.
- It can make some people anxious, dizzy, or more nauseated, especially when they're already dehydrated and run-down.
- In people who use cannabis heavily and often, it can cause a condition with repeated, severe vomiting (cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome), the opposite of what you want.
- If you're still a bit drunk from the night before, adding another substance that slows your reactions isn't wise.

If you never use cannabis, a hangover morning is not the time to start. If you do, know that it isn't treating the hangover itself.

### Spicy Sichuan food: a matter of taste and stomach

Hot, spicy food is a hangover tradition in many cultures, and there's some logic to it. A big, brothy, salty meal brings fluid, sodium, and calories. Spice makes your nose run and your eyes water, which can feel like a reset. Food in general also helps bring blood sugar back up.

The problem is Sichuan cooking in particular. Chili and Sichuan peppercorn on an already-inflamed stomach can bring on heartburn, stomach pain, and diarrhea. If your hangover is mostly a headache and tiredness, spicy noodles might feel great. If your hangover is mostly nausea or acid, start with something bland and save the chili oil for later.

### The Bourdain verdict

Bourdain's cure gets two things genuinely right: a proper pain reliever and a sugary, caffeinated drink. The food is a reasonable idea in a milder form. The joint is personal preference with real downsides. Overall, it's a better hangover plan than most celebrity versions, as long as you add plenty of water and treat the chili as optional.

## The Prairie Oyster (and Jeeves's Pick-Me-Up)

The prairie oyster is the classic "brace yourself" hangover cure: a raw egg yolk dropped whole into a glass with Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce, salt, and pepper, swallowed in one go. Some versions add a splash of tomato juice, vinegar, or brandy.

It's famous partly because of fiction. In P. G. Wodehouse's stories, the unflappable butler Jeeves wins Bertie Wooster over with a restorative morning drink made with raw egg, Worcestershire sauce, and red pepper, and the drink has been linked to Jeeves ever since. A prairie oyster also turns up in the film *Cabaret*.

**What might help:** The egg yolk adds a little protein and fat. Eggs contain cysteine, an amino acid that helps the body make glutathione, which the liver uses to process acetaldehyde, though one yolk provides only a small amount. The salt in Worcestershire and hot sauce adds a little sodium.

**What doesn't:** The quantities are tiny. You'd get far more from a cooked egg breakfast and a glass of water. The "shock" of swallowing it whole is the main event, and that does nothing for your body. Raw eggs also carry a small risk of salmonella. That's a bad trade on a morning when your stomach is already fragile. If you like the idea, our guide to [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains how to get the same nutrients without the raw egg.

**Verdict:** Mostly theater. Cook the egg.

## Kingsley Amis and the "Metaphysical Hangover"

The British novelist Kingsley Amis wrote at length about drinking, including a well-known essay on hangovers in his book *On Drink* (1972). His most lasting idea was splitting the hangover into two parts: the **physical hangover** (the headache, nausea, and exhaustion) and the **metaphysical hangover** (the gloom, guilt, anxiety, and sense of doom that can come with it).

His physical advice was a mix of the sensible and the comic: rest, a shower, getting your body moving, and, if circumstances allowed, sex. For the metaphysical side, he suggested leaning into it with serious, sad reading and music rather than trying to cheer yourself up.

**What holds up:** The two-part split is genuinely useful, and it's now recognized in its own way. The anxiety and low mood after drinking, nicknamed "hangxiety," are common. Part of it comes from your brain chemistry rebounding as alcohol wears off, and part from poor sleep. Recognizing that the dread is partly chemical can make it easier to ride out. A shower and gentle movement can help you feel more human, too.

**What doesn't:** None of it shortens the hangover. Amis was writing as an entertainer as much as an adviser, and much of the essay is a joke at the drinker's expense.

**Verdict:** The best writing on hangovers, and the "metaphysical hangover" idea is a real insight. As medicine, it's mostly about coping rather than cure.

## Hair of the Dog Cocktails: Bloody Mary, Corpse Reviver, and Friends

Several of the most famous cocktails were invented, or at least marketed, as morning-after cures. The idea, "hair of the dog that bit you," is that a little more alcohol eases the hangover.

### The Bloody Mary

Vodka, tomato juice, lemon, Worcestershire, hot sauce, celery salt, and pepper. Its origin story is disputed, with bartenders in Paris and New York both credited at different times. It became the definitive brunch hangover drink.

The non-alcoholic parts aren't bad: tomato juice gives fluid, some potassium, and a little sugar, and the seasonings add salt. A Virgin Mary keeps all of that. The vodka is the part that "works," and only in the short term.

### The Corpse Reviver No. 2

Gin, Cointreau, Lillet (or a similar aperitif wine), lemon juice, and a dash of absinthe. It belongs to a family of "corpse reviver" drinks designed to get you going in the morning. The 1930 *Savoy Cocktail Book* by bartender Harry Craddock famously warned that four of them taken in quick succession would "unrevive the corpse again." That line is as good a summary of hair-of-the-dog logic as any.

### Why the hair of the dog feels like it works

A small drink can briefly blunt hangover symptoms. Part of the hangover is your body readjusting as alcohol leaves your system, and adding more alcohol postpones that readjustment. Alcohol also dulls pain and lifts mood for a while.

But you aren't fixing anything. You're pushing the hangover later in the day and adding more alcohol for your liver to process, which often means a longer and worse crash. Making it a habit is a warning sign, because needing a drink to feel normal in the morning can be an early marker of physical dependence. Our deep dive on [whether hair of the dog works](/never-hungover/does-hair-of-the-dog-work) goes through the research in detail.

**Verdict:** It delays the hangover; it doesn't cure it. Order the virgin version and keep the good parts.

## Traditional Hangover Foods From Around the World

Many cultures have their own famous hangover food, and these are, as a group, the most sensible cures on this list. Most are hot, salty, brothy dishes, which is what a dehydrated, depleted body actually needs.

| Cure | Where | What's in it | What might help | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Menudo | Mexico | Tripe soup with hominy, chili, lime, onion | Fluid, salt, protein, slow carbs | Rich and spicy; can be heavy on a queasy stomach |
| Haejangguk ("soup to chase a hangover") | South Korea | Beef broth, cabbage, bean sprouts, sometimes congealed blood | Fluid, salt, easy calories; bean sprouts are a source of asparagine, an amino acid studied in hangover research | Heat level varies |
| Pho | Vietnam | Beef or chicken broth, rice noodles, herbs | Gentle on the stomach, fluid, salt, easy carbs | Chili and sriracha are optional for a reason |
| Pickle brine (rassol) | Russia, Poland, Eastern Europe | Juice from salt-brined cucumbers | Sodium and fluid | Very salty; acidic; not for people watching blood pressure |
| Rollmops / "hangover breakfast" | Germany | Pickled herring, onions, gherkins | Salt, protein | Strong flavors if you're nauseated |
| Işkembe çorbası | Turkey | Tripe soup with garlic and vinegar | Fluid, salt, protein | Garlic and vinegar can sting a sore stomach |
| Irn-Bru | Scotland | Sugary, caffeinated soft drink | Sugar, caffeine, fluid | Basically Bourdain's Coke in another color |
| Umeboshi | Japan | Salty pickled plum, often with tea or rice porridge | Salt and something easy to eat | Very salty |

A few of these have a little research interest behind them. Korean scientists have studied bean sprout extracts and the amino acids in them for effects on alcohol processing, mostly in lab and animal work. A small Australian study from the national science agency CSIRO found that Korean pear juice taken *before* drinking reduced some hangover symptoms, though it was a small, preliminary trial and didn't test pear juice after the fact. None of this proves the traditional dishes work beyond what you'd expect from any salty soup.

What these dishes really have in common is simpler: fluid, sodium, warm food that's easy to digest, and a ritual that gets you sitting down and eating. That covers dehydration, low blood sugar, and an empty stomach, three of the main hangover drivers. For our ranked list of the best options, see [the best soups for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-soups-for-hangover).

**Verdict:** The best category of famous cure. Pick the gentlest version your stomach can handle.

## Ancient and Strange Cures

Hangovers are as old as drinking, and so are the remedies. A few that turn up in histories of the hangover:

- **Cabbage.** Ancient Greek and Roman writers recommended cabbage for drinking problems, both before and after. Cabbage is mostly water with some vitamins, so it's harmless, but there's no good evidence it helps a hangover.
- **Willow bark.** Ancient healers used willow bark for pain and fever. It contains salicin, the natural compound related to aspirin. In that sense, the ancients were onto the same idea as Bourdain's Advil.
- **Raw owl eggs and other ordeals.** Roman sources, including Pliny the Elder, describe strange concoctions meant to put people off wine altogether. These were aversion remedies as much as cures, and they don't help.
- **Lemon under the armpit.** A folk remedy often linked to Puerto Rico: rubbing a lemon wedge under the arm on the drinking arm. There's no plausible way it could work, though it does no harm.
- **Sweating it out.** Saunas, steam rooms, and hard workouts are a popular modern version. You can't sweat out alcohol in meaningful amounts, and heat plus exercise when you're already dehydrated can make you dizzy or faint. Our guide on [whether exercise helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-exercise-help-a-hangover) covers what's safe.

## Viral and Modern Celebrity Cures

Every few months a new hangover hack goes viral, often attached to a celebrity or influencer. Pickle juice shots, IV drip bars, hangover patches, activated charcoal, and electrolyte powders all have their moment. Our separate review of [viral hangover cures](/never-hungover/viral-hangover-cures-tested-science-2025) checks the evidence for each.

The same rule applies to all of them as to the classics: look for the part that delivers fluid, salt, sugar, food, sleep, or a proper painkiller, and treat everything else as decoration. If a product claims to "cure" or "eliminate" hangovers, be skeptical. The research doesn't support any claim that strong.

## The Famous Cures, Scored

| Cure | What it gets right | What it gets wrong | Worth trying? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bourdain: Advil | Treats headache and inflammation | Hard on a sore stomach; never with heavy daily drinking | Yes, one label dose with food |
| Bourdain: cold Coke | Fluid, sugar, caffeine | No real electrolytes; acidic | Yes, alongside water |
| Bourdain: joint | Some find it relaxing | No evidence; can worsen nausea or anxiety; legal issues | Not recommended |
| Bourdain: Sichuan food | Salt, fluid, calories | Spice can inflame an upset stomach | If your stomach is fine |
| Prairie oyster | A little protein and salt | Raw egg risk; tiny amounts | Cook the egg instead |
| Amis's advice | Names the "hangxiety" problem; shower and rest | Doesn't speed recovery | As a coping guide |
| Bloody Mary / Corpse Reviver | Tomato juice, salt (Bloody Mary) | The alcohol only delays the hangover | Virgin versions only |
| Hangover soups (menudo, pho, haejangguk) | Fluid, salt, easy food | Spicy versions can upset the stomach | Yes, the best of the lot |
| Pickle brine | Sodium and fluid | Very salty and acidic | A few sips, with water |
| Sweating it out | Nothing reliable | Worsens dehydration | No |

## What Actually Helps a Hangover

If you strip the famous cures down to their useful parts, you end up with a short, unglamorous list:

1. **Fluids, ideally with some salt.** Water is good. An oral rehydration drink or a salty broth is better if you've been sick or sweating. Our guide to the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares the options.
2. **Real food.** Eggs, toast, a bowl of soup, rice, or a banana. Bland if you're queasy, heartier once you're steady. See our list of the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover).
3. **One proper pain reliever, used correctly.** Ibuprofen with food for a headache, or acetaminophen at a normal dose if you're not a heavy daily drinker and haven't taken other products containing it.
4. **Something for nausea.** Small sips of a cold drink or ginger can help. Our guide to [ginger for a hangover](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) explains the evidence.
5. **Caffeine, in moderation,** if you're a regular coffee drinker.
6. **Sleep.** The single biggest factor in feeling better. A nap does more than any cure.
7. **Time.** Most hangovers fade within about a day.

And the most reliable "cure" of all is prevention: drinking less, slowing down, eating before and while you drink, and alternating alcoholic drinks with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Where Supplements Like DHM Fit

Some people add a supplement on nights they plan to drink. The most talked-about is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, used in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries. Lab and animal studies suggest it may support the enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde, and it has been studied for liver health, including a small 2015 human trial in people with fatty liver disease. Human evidence specifically on hangovers is still limited, so it's best seen as a promising option rather than a proven one. There is no good evidence that DHM, or any supplement, cures a hangover once you have one, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe.

If you'd like to try it, it's typically taken while drinking or before bed rather than the next morning. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Think of it as one small piece alongside water, food, and pacing, not a replacement for them.

## The Bottom Line

- Anthony Bourdain's hangover cure is half good advice: the Advil and cold Coke help, the spicy food depends on your stomach, and the joint is best skipped.
- The prairie oyster is mostly theater; a cooked egg and a glass of water do the same job better and more safely.
- Kingsley Amis's "metaphysical hangover" is a real and useful idea, but his advice is about coping, not curing.
- Hair-of-the-dog cocktails like the Bloody Mary and Corpse Reviver only postpone the hangover.
- Traditional hangover soups from around the world are the most sensible famous cures because they deliver fluid, salt, and easy food.
- No famous cure shortens a hangover in any proven way. Fluids, food, a painkiller used correctly, sleep, and time do the work.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What was Anthony Bourdain's hangover cure?**

Bourdain's widely quoted hangover cure was Advil, a large cold Coca-Cola, a joint, and a big bowl of spicy Sichuan food. The exact wording varies by source, but those four parts are always included. The ibuprofen and the Coke are the most useful parts, since they ease a headache and provide fluid, sugar, and caffeine. The spicy food can help or hurt depending on your stomach, and the joint has no good evidence behind it as a hangover treatment.

**Does Anthony Bourdain's hangover cure actually work?**

Partly. Ibuprofen is a real pain reliever that also works against inflammation, and a cold Coke supplies fluid, quick sugar, and caffeine, which can make you feel noticeably better. But it doesn't speed up recovery, and the spicy food and cannabis can worsen nausea or heartburn for some people. Add plenty of water, take the ibuprofen with food, and treat the chili as optional.

**What is a prairie oyster hangover cure?**

A prairie oyster is a raw egg yolk swallowed whole with Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce, salt, and pepper. It's famous from P. G. Wodehouse's Jeeves stories and films like Cabaret. It provides a tiny amount of protein and salt, but the raw egg carries a small salmonella risk, and a cooked egg with a glass of water gives you more of the same nutrients more safely.

**Is a Bloody Mary good for a hangover?**

The tomato juice and seasonings provide fluid, some potassium, and salt, which are genuinely useful. The vodka is what makes you feel better in the short term, but it only postpones the hangover and gives your liver more to process. A Virgin Mary keeps the helpful parts without the alcohol. Regularly needing a drink to feel normal in the morning is worth discussing with a doctor.

**What is the best hangover food from around the world?**

Hot, salty, brothy soups are the most sensible traditional cures. Examples include Mexican menudo, Korean haejangguk, and Vietnamese pho. They replace fluid and sodium and give you easy-to-digest food, which covers three main hangover problems at once. If you're nauseated, choose the mildest version and skip extra chili until your stomach settles.

**Is there any hangover cure that actually works?**

There is no good evidence that any single remedy cures a hangover. A 2005 systematic review in the BMJ found no compelling evidence for any of the hangover remedies tested in controlled trials up to that point, and that broad picture hasn't changed. What reliably helps is easing the symptoms: fluids with some salt, food, a pain reliever used correctly, sleep, and time. The most effective approach is prevention, which means drinking less and more slowly, eating, and drinking water between drinks.

**When should I see a doctor for a hangover?**

Get help right away if someone can't keep fluids down for many hours, vomits blood, is confused or hard to wake, has a seizure, has slow or irregular breathing, or has chest pain or a racing heart that won't settle. Those can be signs of alcohol poisoning or another emergency. If you regularly feel shaky, sweaty, and anxious on mornings after drinking and only a drink settles it, talk to a doctor, since that can be an early sign of alcohol withdrawal rather than a normal hangover.
